question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

No student will be allowed to (a)/ appear in the final examination (b)/ unless he does not clear (c)/ all the pending library dues. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Unless" already has a negative meaning ("if … not"), so it is not used with another negative word. So "unless he does not clear" must be "unless he clears".

◦ Corrected sentence: No student will be allowed to appear in the final examination unless he clears all the pending library dues.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "No student will be allowed to" is proper, with the singular "student" after "No" and the passive "will be allowed to".

 

• Part (b) is correct — "appear in the final examination" is proper, with "appear in" used for an examination.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "all the pending library dues." is proper, with "all the" used before the plural noun "dues".

 

NOTE

 

• unless he pays, unless she comes (unless + an affirmative verb), and not unless he does not pay; if he does not pay has the same meaning as unless he pays.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

Both the manager as well as (a)/ his assistant were held responsible (b)/ for the huge loss. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Both" is paired with "and" and not with "as well as". So "Both the manager as well as" must be "Both the manager and".

◦ Corrected sentence: Both the manager and his assistant were held responsible for the huge loss.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "his assistant were held responsible" is proper, with the plural verb "were" after "both … and" and "held responsible" used in the passive.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "for the huge loss." is proper, with "for" showing the cause and "the" used before a specific loss.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "Both … as well as" in part (a) uses the wrong pair of conjunctions.

 

NOTE

 

• Both the teacher and the students (both … and); The teacher as well as the students (as well as, without "both").

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

The football match was called off (a)/ because heavy rain and waterlogging (b)/ on the ground. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Because" is a conjunction and is followed by a clause (subject + verb). Before a noun phrase, "because of" is used. "Heavy rain and waterlogging" is a noun phrase, so "because" must be "because of".

◦ Corrected sentence: The football match was called off because of heavy rain and waterlogging on the ground.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The football match was called off" is proper, with the passive "was called off" meaning "was cancelled".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "on the ground." is proper, with "on" used for the surface of the ground.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "because" in part (b) is followed by a noun phrase and not a clause.

 

NOTE

 

• because it rained (because + clause); because of the rain, because of his illness (because of + noun).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The new policy aims to both (a)/ increase farmers' income (b)/ and reducing the burden (c)/ of agricultural loans. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The two items joined by "both … and" must be in the same grammatical form (parallel structure). "Increase" is a base verb, so "reducing" must be "reduce".

◦ Corrected sentence: The new policy aims to both increase farmers' income and reduce the burden of agricultural loans.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The new policy aims to both" is proper, with "aims to" followed by a base verb and "both" placed before the first item.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "increase farmers' income" is proper, with the base verb "increase" and the possessive "farmers'".

 

• Part (d) is correct — "of agricultural loans." is proper, with "burden of" followed by a noun phrase.

 

NOTE

 

• both to save and to spend, both increase and reduce (the same form on both sides of "both … and").

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

No sooner had the results been announced (a)/ when the students rushed (b)/ to the notice board. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "No sooner" is followed by "than", while "hardly" and "scarcely" are followed by "when". So "when the students rushed" must be "than the students rushed".

◦ Corrected sentence: No sooner had the results been announced than the students rushed to the notice board.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "No sooner had the results been announced" is proper, with "had" placed before the subject after "No sooner" and the past perfect passive.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "to the notice board." is proper, with "to" showing direction.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "when" in part (b) does not go with "No sooner".

 

NOTE

 

• No sooner had he left than it began to rain; Hardly had he left when it began to rain ("no sooner … than", "hardly … when").

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The organisers have installed large screens (a)/ in the hall and around the campus (b)/ for the visitors (c)/ that everyone can watch the event clearly. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A purpose clause is introduced by "so that" (or "in order that"), and "that" alone is not used for it. So "that everyone can watch" must be "so that everyone can watch".

◦ Corrected sentence: The organisers have installed large screens in the hall and around the campus for the visitors so that everyone can watch the event clearly.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The organisers have installed large screens" is proper, with the plural verb "have" agreeing with "organisers" and the present perfect for a recent action.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "in the hall and around the campus" is proper, with "in" used for a place and "around" for the surrounding area.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "for the visitors" is proper, with "for" showing who benefits.

 

NOTE

 

• He ran fast so that he could catch the bus, She spoke slowly so that everyone could follow (so that + a clause showing purpose).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

Hardly had the guests taken their seats than (a)/ the lights went out (b)/ and the whole hall (c)/ was plunged into darkness. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Hardly" and "scarcely" are followed by "when" (or "before"), and "than" is used only after "no sooner" or a comparative. So "than" must be "when".

◦ Corrected sentence: Hardly had the guests taken their seats when the lights went out and the whole hall was plunged into darkness.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "the lights went out" is proper, with the simple past "went out" in the clause after "when".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "and the whole hall" is proper, with "and" joining the two events and "the whole" before a singular noun.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "was plunged into darkness." is proper, with the passive "was plunged" and "into" showing change of state.

 

NOTE

 

• Hardly had he arrived when it began to rain; No sooner had he arrived than it began to rain.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The children (a)/ wore the same uniform (b)/ like the one their (c)/ elder brothers had worn. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Same" is followed by "as" (or "that") and not by "like". So "like the one" must be "as the one".

◦ Corrected sentence: The children wore the same uniform as the one their elder brothers had worn.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The children" is proper, as a plural subject that agrees with the verb "wore".

 

• Part (b) is correct — "wore the same uniform" is proper, with "the same" placed before a noun.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "elder brothers had worn." is proper, with "elder" used for older siblings and the past perfect for an earlier action.

 

NOTE

 

• the same book as mine, the same shirt that I wore (same … as / that), and not the same book like mine.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

He is neither honest (a)/ or hardworking, (b)/ yet the manager trusts him. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Neither" is paired with "nor" and not with "or". So "or hardworking" must be "nor hardworking".

◦ Corrected sentence: He is neither honest nor hardworking, yet the manager trusts him.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "He is neither honest" is proper, with "neither" placed before the first adjective.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "yet the manager trusts him." is proper, with "yet" showing contrast.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "or" in part (b) does not go with "neither".

 

NOTE

 

• neither … nor, either … or, both … and, not only … but also (fixed pairs).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

Not only did the company (a)/ raise the salaries, but it also (b)/ improved the working conditions. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence is grammatically correct. When a sentence begins with "Not only", the auxiliary comes before the subject ("did the company raise"), and the second part follows with "but … also".

◦ Sentence as given: Not only did the company raise the salaries, but it also improved the working conditions.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Not only did the company" is proper, with the inversion "did + subject" after "Not only".

 

• Part (b) is correct — "raise the salaries, but it also" is proper, with the base verb "raise" after "did" and "but … also" completing the pair.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "improved the working conditions." is proper, with the simple past "improved" in the second clause.

 

NOTE

 

• Not only did he win, but he also broke the record (inversion after a sentence-initial "Not only").

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

Although the team played brilliantly, but (a)/ it could not win the (b)/ trophy this season. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Although / though" already shows contrast, so "but" is not used in the main clause of the same sentence. So "Although the team played brilliantly, but" must be "Although the team played brilliantly,".

◦ Corrected sentence: Although the team played brilliantly, it could not win the trophy this season.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "it could not win the" is proper, with "could not" followed by the base verb "win".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "trophy this season." is proper, because "this season" takes no preposition.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "but" in part (a) is used together with "Although".

 

NOTE

 

• Although he tried, he failed; He tried, but he failed (one contrast word only), and not Although he tried, but he failed.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The young violinist's performance (a)/ at the annual festival was (b)/ such impressive that the entire hall (c)/ gave her a standing ovation. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "So" is used before an adjective or adverb ("so impressive that"), while "such" is used before a noun ("such an impressive performance that"). So "such impressive that" must be "so impressive that".

◦ Corrected sentence: The young violinist's performance at the annual festival was so impressive that the entire hall gave her a standing ovation.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The young violinist's performance" is proper, with the possessive "violinist's" before the noun "performance".

 

• Part (b) is correct — "at the annual festival was" is proper, with "at" used for an event and the singular "was" agreeing with "performance".

 

• Part (d) is correct — "gave her a standing ovation." is proper, with the simple past "gave" and the fixed phrase "a standing ovation".

 

NOTE

 

• so tired that, so fast that (so + adjective / adverb + that); such a tall boy that, such a long journey that (such + a / an + noun).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The old man was so weak to climb (a)/ the stairs without support, (b)/ so his son (c)/ helped him. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Too + adjective + to + verb" shows that something is not possible, while "so … that" is followed by a full clause. "So weak to climb" is a mixture of both, so it must be "too weak to climb".

◦ Corrected sentence: The old man was too weak to climb the stairs without support, so his son helped him.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "the stairs without support," is proper, with "without" followed by a noun.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "so his son" is proper, with "so" introducing the result.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "helped him." is proper, with the simple past "helped" and the object pronoun "him".

 

NOTE

 

• too weak to walk, too tired to speak (too + adjective + to); so weak that he could not walk (so + adjective + that + clause).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

The paper was extremely difficult because most students scored very high marks in the examination.
option_2: because most students scored very high marks
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. because most students scored very high marks.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The two facts are opposite in meaning ("extremely difficult" and "very high marks"), so a contrast conjunction such as "yet" or "but" is needed, and "because" (which gives a reason) is wrong. So "because most students scored" must be "yet most students scored".

◦ Corrected sentence: The paper was extremely difficult yet most students scored very high marks in the examination.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "The paper was extremely difficult" — this part is correct, with the singular verb "was" and the adverb "extremely" modifying "difficult".

 

• Option 3: "in the examination." — this part is correct, with "in" used before "the examination".

 

• Option 4: No error — incorrect, because "because" in option 2 joins two contrasting ideas.

 

NOTE

 

• It was hard, yet he passed, The task was tough but she finished it (contrast: yet / but), and not It was hard because he passed.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

Despite the doctor had warned him about the risk, he refused to take rest.
option_1: Despite the doctor had warned him
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Despite the doctor had warned him.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Despite" and "In spite of" are prepositions and are followed by a noun or a gerund, and not by a full clause. Before a clause, "although / though / even though" is used. So "Despite the doctor had warned him" must be "Although the doctor had warned him".

◦ Corrected sentence: Although the doctor had warned him about the risk, he refused to take rest.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "about the risk," — this part is correct, with "warned him about" followed by a noun phrase.

 

• Option 3: "he refused" — this part is correct, with the simple past "refused" in the main clause.

 

• Option 4: "to take rest." — this part is correct, with "refuse" followed by a to-infinitive.

 

NOTE

 

• Although he was ill, he came; Despite his illness, he came; Despite being ill, he came (a clause after "although", a noun / gerund after "despite").

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

We stayed on the lawn till midnight because it was so a pleasant evening.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. so a pleasant evening.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "So" is used before an adjective or adverb without an article ("so pleasant"), while "such + a / an + adjective + noun" is used before a noun. So "so a pleasant evening" must be "such a pleasant evening" (or "so pleasant an evening").

◦ Corrected sentence: We stayed on the lawn till midnight because it was such a pleasant evening.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "We stayed on the lawn" — this part is correct, with the simple past "stayed" and "on" used for a lawn.

 

• Option 2: "till midnight" — this part is correct, with "till" used before a point of time.

 

• Option 3: "because it was" — this part is correct, with "because" introducing the reason and the singular "was" agreeing with "it".

 

NOTE

 

• such a lovely day, such an easy question (such + a / an + adjective + noun); so lovely a day (so + adjective + a / an + noun).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

The new smartphone is costly but it is not as durable than the old one.
option_3: not as durable than the old one.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. not as durable than the old one.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In a comparison of equality, the pattern is "as … as" ("not as durable as"), and "than" is used only after a comparative degree ("more durable than"). So "not as durable than" must be "not as durable as".

◦ Corrected sentence: The new smartphone is costly but it is not as durable as the old one.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "The new smartphone is costly" — this part is correct, with the singular verb "is" and the adjective "costly".

 

• Option 2: "but it is" — this part is correct, with "but" showing contrast and "it" referring to the smartphone.

 

• Option 4: No error — incorrect, because "than" in option 3 does not go with "as durable".

 

NOTE

 

• not as durable as, as tall as (as … as); more durable than, taller than (comparative + than).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

The scholarship will be awarded either to Meera and to the winner of the national quiz.
option_3: to the winner of the national quiz.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. awarded either to Meera and.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Either" is paired with "or" and not with "and". So "either to Meera and" must be "either to Meera or".

◦ Corrected sentence: The scholarship will be awarded either to Meera or to the winner of the national quiz.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "The scholarship will be" — this part is correct, with the passive future "will be awarded" completed in the next part.

 

• Option 3: "to the winner of the national quiz." — this part is correct, with "to" repeated for parallel structure and "the winner of" a specific person.

 

• Option 4: No error — incorrect, because "and" in option 2 does not go with "either".

 

NOTE

 

• either Ravi or Mohan, either to Meera or to Sita (either … or), and not either … and.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

Vegetable prices have shot up (a)/ during the last two weeks, (b)/ and the main reason (c)/ is because heavy rains destroyed the crops. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After "the reason … is / was", the conjunction "that" is used, and "because" is not used, because "reason" already shows cause. So "is because" must be "is that".

◦ Corrected sentence: Vegetable prices have shot up during the last two weeks, and the main reason is that heavy rains destroyed the crops.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Vegetable prices have shot up" is proper, with the plural verb "have" and the present perfect for a recent change.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "during the last two weeks," is proper, with "during" followed by a specific period.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "and the main reason" is proper, with "and" joining the two clauses and "the main reason" as the subject.

 

NOTE

 

• The reason is that he was late, The reason for the delay was that the train was late (reason … that), and not The reason is because.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The judge asked that whether (a)/ the witness had seen (b)/ the accused at the (c)/ scene of the crime. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In indirect speech, the reporting verb "asked" is followed directly by "whether / if", and "that" is not used with them. So "asked that whether" must be "asked whether".

◦ Corrected sentence: The judge asked whether the witness had seen the accused at the scene of the crime.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (b) is correct — "the witness had seen" is proper, with the past perfect after the past reporting verb "asked".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "the accused at the" is proper, with "the accused" used for a person charged with a crime.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "scene of the crime." is proper, with "scene of" used before the place of an event.

 

NOTE

 

• She asked me whether I was ready, He asked if she had come (asked + whether / if), and not asked that whether, asked that if.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The company will hire (a)/ such candidates who (b)/ have completed (c)/ the advanced course. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Such" is followed by "as" used as a relative pronoun ("such … as"), and "who" is not used after "such". So "such candidates who" must be "such candidates as".

◦ Corrected sentence: The company will hire such candidates as have completed the advanced course.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The company will hire" is proper, with the simple future "will hire" and a singular subject.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "have completed" is proper, with the plural verb "have" agreeing with "candidates".

 

• Part (d) is correct — "the advanced course." is proper, with "the" used before a specific course.

 

NOTE

 

• such books as are useful, such men as work hard (such … as), and not such books which are useful; the same … as / that follows a similar pattern.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The committee will meet on Friday (a)/ to discuss (b)/ if to postpone the annual fair (c)/ because of the floods. (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (c).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "If" cannot be followed by a to-infinitive. To show a choice between two courses of action, "whether + to-infinitive" is used. So "if to postpone" must be "whether to postpone".

◦ Corrected sentence: The committee will meet on Friday to discuss whether to postpone the annual fair because of the floods.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The committee will meet on Friday" is proper, with "on" used before a day.

 

• Part (b) is correct — "to discuss" is proper, because "discuss" is a transitive verb and takes no preposition.

 

• Part (d) is correct — "because of the floods." is proper, with "because of" followed by a noun phrase.

 

NOTE

 

• She could not decide whether to accept, He asked me whether to wait (whether + to-infinitive), and not if to accept, if to wait.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

Hardly had the singer finished (a)/ the first song when the (b)/ audience began to cheer. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. (d).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence is grammatically correct. "Hardly" is followed by the past perfect with "had" before the subject, and the second clause is joined by "when", so "Hardly had the singer finished … when the audience began" is correct.

◦ Sentence as given: Hardly had the singer finished the first song when the audience began to cheer.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "Hardly had the singer finished" is proper, with "had" placed before the subject after "Hardly" and the past participle "finished".

 

• Part (b) is correct — "the first song when the" is proper, with "when" joining the second clause to "Hardly".

 

• Part (c) is correct — "audience began to cheer." is proper, with the simple past "began" in the clause after "when".

 

NOTE

 

• Hardly had she entered when the bell rang; Scarcely had they left when it began to snow (hardly / scarcely … when).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

The protesters managed to (a)/ reach the gates despite of (b)/ the heavy security. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (b).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Despite" is never followed by "of", while the full form is "in spite of". So "despite of" must be "despite" (or "in spite of").

◦ Corrected sentence: The protesters managed to reach the gates despite the heavy security.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (a) is correct — "The protesters managed to" is proper, with "managed to" followed by a base verb.

 

• Part (c) is correct — "the heavy security." is proper, with "the" used before a specific noun.

 

• Option (d) No error — cannot be selected, because "despite of" in part (b) wrongly adds "of" after "despite".

 

NOTE

 

• despite the rain, in spite of the rain (despite / in spite of), and not despite of the rain.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. If the sentence is free from error, select 'No error'.

 

Please do not leave the hall until the invigilator does not collect (a)/ all the answer sheets (b)/ from the students. (c)/ No error (d)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (a).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Until", like "unless", already has a negative sense ("up to the time when"), so it is not used with another negative word. So "until the invigilator does not collect" must be "until the invigilator collects".

◦ Corrected sentence: Please do not leave the hall until the invigilator collects all the answer sheets from the students.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.
